problems.stem: A readiness review reads: "Everything looks good, we are ready to launch the AI tutor next week." What makes this a weak review?
options: It is too optimistic about students.
It is a rubber stamp: it does not check each prior artifact against a go or no-go criterion.
problems.explanation: A readiness review is a gate. Asserting readiness without an item-by-item check skips the actual work.

problems.stem: During the review the consent forms for the AI tutor have not gone home. What should the readiness verdict be on that item?
options: Go, because consent can be handled later.
No-go on that item: launch is blocked until opt-out paths and the low-tech fallback are in place.
Go, because the rest of the items passed.
problems.explanation: A gate must be able to fail. An unmet blocking item like unsent consent forms returns a no-go.

problems.stem: Someone proposes launching the AI tutor now and gathering consent afterward. Why is this not acceptable?
options: It would take too long to write the memo.
It reverses the policy boundary: consent and the low-tech fallback must be in place before any launch.
It would make the review shorter.
Launching early is fine if students agree.
problems.explanation: Launch-then-comply reverses the consent boundary. The review must reject it.

problems.stem: Which readiness verdict is most auditable by a mentor teacher?
options: Go on the tension map (08.01), tool-boundary transcript (08.02), and rubric (08.04); no-go on policy until consent and the 08.06 fallback are in place; conditional on collecting the 08.07 baseline before week 1.
problems.explanation: The strongest verdict ties each go, no-go, and conditional to the specific prior artifact that justifies it.

problems.stem: Provide a concise response that demonstrates this learning objective: Document a bounded AI/software support move with accepted and rejected suggestions.
problems.expected_answer: The response accurately demonstrates the section objective: Document a bounded AI/software support move with accepted and rejected suggestions, using relevant section concepts, evidence, or calculations.
problems.explanation: This direct-evidence item is used when no closed-response item adequately samples the objective. Score it with the section concepts and worked examples as the rubric.
